clue.text: Friar's dance scoffed at by school boys

parts.note: Friar Tuck is Robin Hood's jolly companion
a hop is an informal dance

explanation.surface: Schoolboys mock the steps a friar performs at a dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scoffed' is not mockery but eating greedily: a TUCK SHOP is a British school's snack shop, where pupils buy sweets and cakes.
explanation.definitionFit: A school snack kiosk is where pupils buy food to wolf down, so it is the place things are scoffed.

clue.text: Beauty-spot on the way is dramatic

definitions.note: the answer is the title of a Shakespeare drama, so the clue calls it dramatic

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece on another sits above it

parts.note: the Vale of Tempe is a famously lovely valley in Greece
St is the abbreviation for street, a way

explanation.surface: A scenic spot beside the road is spectacular.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beauty-spot' looks like a mole on a face but is the Vale of Tempe in Greece. The definition leans on the play title: a storm, but also a drama.
explanation.definitionFit: Besides a violent storm, this is Shakespeare's last solo play, so the word names a drama.

clue.text: Am I unable to join fifty in church's hymns?

parts.note: can't I asks am I unable

indicators.note: fifty goes in the church's letters

parts.note: CE is the Church of England, with S from the possessive
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: A churchgoer wonders if they can't join fifty others in the hymns.
explanation.walkthrough: CE stands for the Church of England, and its possessive 's adds the S.
explanation.definitionFit: Canticles are hymns or chants with biblical texts sung in church services.

clue.text: To a small extent, losing pound is attractive

indicators.note: losing means the word for a small extent drops a letter

parts.note: slightly means a little
L is the abbreviation for pound sterling, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: Losing a bit of weight makes someone a little more attractive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pound' is the money abbreviation L, taken out of SLIGHTLY.
explanation.definitionFit: Sightly is an old-fashioned word for pleasing to look at.

clue.text: Heart of Midlothian? Hurried to castle here

indicators.note: the heart of Midlothian is its central pair of letters

parts.note: ran means hurried

explanation.surface: A Hearts fan dashed to the castle.
explanation.walkthrough: Heart of Midlothian is a Scottish football club, but here it asks for the middle of 'Midlothian'. Walpole's Gothic novel is The Castle of Otranto.
explanation.definitionFit: Horace Walpole set the first Gothic novel in a castle in this southern Italian town.

clue.text: Compared with left half in best team

indicators.note: the left half of a word is its first two of four letters, taken from the word best

parts.note: a side is a sports team

explanation.surface: A footballer's position assessed against the best line-up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left half' looks like the old football position, but it asks for the left-hand half of 'best'.
explanation.definitionFit: Beside can mean in comparison with, as in 'beside her, he looks small'.

clue.text: Balkan statesman rejects right of ruling Arab coalition

indicators.note: a coalition of the letters brings them together in a new combination
the word ruling rejects, throws out, a letter

explanation.surface: A Balkan politician breaks with the Arab alliance's ruling party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejects' drops the R from RULING to give ULING, and 'coalition' mixes ULING with ARAB.
explanation.definitionFit: A statesman from Sofia's country is a native of that Balkan state.

clue.text: Thrift makes one almost see red, say

indicators.note: say means the phrase for nearly seeing red is heard as a different pair of words

parts.note: to almost see red is to see pink, a shade just short of red

explanation.surface: Being thrifty makes someone nearly see red, apparently.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thrift' looks like frugality but is the coastal plant. Seeing pink is almost seeing red, and 'say' turns 'see' into SEA.
explanation.definitionFit: Thrift is a cliff-top plant with pink flowers, also known by this seaside name.

clue.text: Thorny problem — without lead you can't win!

definitions.text: Thorny problem — without lead you can't win!

parts.words: Thorny problem — without lead you can't win!
parts.note: a horned predicament, where whichever way you go you lose, like a card player with no good card to lead

explanation.walkthrough: 'Thorny' alludes to the horns of a predicament; 'lead' suggests a card game where no lead is safe.
explanation.definitionFit: A predicament has two 'horns', so it is thorny, and neither choice wins.

clue.text: New angle Maria wanted about firm control

indicators.note: a new version of the letters of angle and Maria is a rearranged one

explanation.surface: Maria wanted a fresh approach to running the company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wanted' is a link; the definition is the phrase 'about firm control', meaning concerning management of a firm.
explanation.definitionFit: Managerial means relating to the running of a business, which is control of a firm.

clue.text: Sound jump by skater — a lot may turn on it

definitions.text: a lot may turn on it

indicators.note: sound at the head of the clue asks for a word spoken like the skating jump

parts.note: an axel is a figure-skating jump with a forward take-off

explanation.surface: A skater lands a solid jump, and much depends on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound' looks like 'solid' describing the jump, but it signals a word heard alike. 'A lot' is a car lot as well as much.
explanation.definitionFit: Wheels rotate on a shaft between them, so a vehicle's weight turns on it.

clue.text: False arrest for exponent of this philosophy

definitions.text: False arrest for exponent of this philosophy

parts.words: False arrest for exponent of this philosophy
parts.note: a follower of this school, which stresses absurdity and individual freedom, might see wrongful detention as typical of an arbitrary universe, as in Kafka's The Trial

explanation.surface: A wrongful arrest of a philosopher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'False' looks like an anagram signal but no letters fit; the clue alludes to the arbitrary arrest of Josef K in Kafka's The Trial, a touchstone of existentialist thought.
explanation.definitionFit: The philosophy of Sartre and Camus holds that existence is absurd and arbitrary, the mood of a man arrested for nothing.

clue.text: Unspeakable cry?

parts.note: Oscar Wilde called fox-hunters 'the unspeakable in full pursuit of the uneatable', so this is the call the unspeakable make

explanation.walkthrough: 'Unspeakable' seems to mean a cry too awful to utter, but it is Wilde's word for fox-hunters.
explanation.definitionFit: The hunting call on sighting a fox is what Wilde's 'unspeakable' huntsmen shout.

clue.text: Poor visibility for Henry on the stairs

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece on another sits above it

parts.note: Hal is the pet name of Henry, as in Shakespeare's Prince Hal
a flight is a set of stairs

explanation.surface: Henry can barely see on the dim staircase.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Henry' looks like H, the unit, but is the nickname HAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Dim twilight gives only partial light, so seeing is poor.

clue.text: Liaison officer as torchbearer

definitions.meaning: someone who connects groups or presents between items
a link was a torch, carried by a man lighting people through dark streets

explanation.surface: A liaison officer doubles as the one holding the torch.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a connecting person, such as a broadcast presenter, and historically a hired lighter of the way carrying a pitch torch.

clue.text: Very little produced by Hilliard

definitions.meaning: Nicholas Hilliard was the Elizabethan painter of tiny portraits

explanation.surface: Hilliard made hardly anything.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means tiny and also names the small portraits on vellum that Hilliard painted for Elizabeth I's court.

clue.text: Elastic construction of Isabella's domain

indicators.note: a construction of the letters of elastic is a fresh build from them

explanation.surface: Isabella's realm built from stretchy material.
explanation.walkthrough: Isabella I of Spain was queen of this kingdom.
explanation.definitionFit: Isabella the Catholic ruled this central Spanish kingdom, which united with Aragon through her marriage.

clue.text: He carefully checks balance in sound receiver

definitions.meaning: a hearer, from Latin audire, to hear

explanation.surface: An inspector checks the balance on a radio set.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names an accountant who checks a firm's balance sheet and, from its Latin root, a listener who takes in sound.

clue.text: Poles understand travel's mainly arranged in inns

indicators.note: arranged means these letters are put in a new order

parts.note: N and S are the north and south poles

indicators.note: mainly means most of the word travel, so its last letter goes

parts.note: the word travel, the possessive adding no letter

explanation.surface: Poles grasp that travel is mostly organised around inns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'understand' acts only as a link; NS and TRAVE (most of 'travel') are mixed by 'arranged'.
explanation.definitionFit: Taverns are pubs or inns serving drink.

clue.text: Shakespearian merchant, or usurper in 1 dn

definitions.meaning: the title character of The Merchant of Venice
1 down is a Shakespeare play in which Prospero's brother seized his dukedom of Milan

explanation.surface: A Shakespeare trader who is also the usurping brother in another play.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare used the same name for the Venetian trader who borrows from Shylock and for Prospero's treacherous brother.

clue.text: Joseph essayed to be a writer

definitions.text: Joseph essayed to be a writer

parts.words: Joseph essayed to be a writer
parts.note: essayed puns on tried and on writing essays: Joseph is the first name of an essayist co-founder of The Spectator

explanation.walkthrough: 'essayed' looks like 'tried' but points to an essay writer.
explanation.definitionFit: Joseph Addison was the eighteenth-century essayist who co-founded The Spectator with Richard Steele.

clue.text: Verse? That's the long and the short of it

definitions.text: Verse? That's the long and the short of it

parts.words: Verse? That's the long and the short of it
parts.note: the metrical foot made of one stressed or long syllable followed by an unstressed or short one

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'the long and the short of it' is taken literally as a pattern of syllables.
explanation.definitionFit: This foot of verse is a long syllable then a short one, literally the long and the short.

clue.text: Cram for odd parts of exam in public

indicators.note: the picked letters go in the word for public

parts.note: overt means open, done in public

indicators.note: the odd parts of exam are its first and third letters

explanation.surface: Swotting for parts of an exam in the open.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cram' looks like last-minute study but means stuffing yourself with food.
explanation.definitionFit: To cram oneself is to stuff in too much food.

clue.text: He finds fault with proposal to lengthen calendar

definitions.text: He finds fault with proposal to lengthen calendar

parts.words: He finds fault with proposal to lengthen calendar
parts.note: in the Catholic Church an official argued against each candidate for sainthood, a proposal that would add a name to the calendar of saints

explanation.walkthrough: The 'calendar' is the Church's calendar of saints' days, lengthened when a new saint is canonised.
explanation.definitionFit: The Church official who opposed canonisations objected to adding saints to the calendar; the title now means anyone arguing the contrary case.

clue.text: Gaol disturbance

explanation.surface: Unrest in a prison.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is slang for prison and also means a commotion, as in causing a stir.

clue.text: Sort of 22 for gardeners

parts.note: 22 across is slang for prison; the military prison has a slang name that is also a gardener's glazed building

explanation.walkthrough: In British army slang a military prison is called by the name of a gardener's greenhouse.
explanation.definitionFit: The glazed building for growing plants shares its name with British army slang for a military prison.

clue.text: Pledge given by Germans

parts.note: a pledge here is a toast to someone's health, and this is the German drinking toast

explanation.walkthrough: 'Pledge' looks like a promise but means drinking someone's health.
explanation.definitionFit: The German and Latin toast meaning 'may it benefit' is what Germans say when raising glasses to pledge health.

clue.text: Improper order about old city address

indicators.note: the word for an order goes about, around, the city postcode

parts.note: an indent is an official order for goods
EC is the postcode of the City of London, the old square mile

explanation.surface: A rude command concerning an old town's location.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Address' is a postal address, the City of London's EC postcode district.
explanation.definitionFit: Indecent behaviour is improper, offending against decency.
